texts.b2dc77b06436: UK Biobank aims to study how the health of 500,000 people, currently aged 40-69, from all around the UK is affected by their lifestyle, environment and genes.  The purpose of this major project is to improve prevention, diagnosis and treatment of a wide range of illnesses (such as cancer, heart disease, diabetes, dementia, and joint problems) and to promote health throughout society.  By analysing answers, measurements and samples collected from participants, researchers may be able to work out why some people develop particular diseases while others do not.  This should help us to find new ways to prevent early death and disability from many different diseases.  Like giving blood, UK Biobank is not intended to help directly those who take part - but it should give future generations a much better chance of living their lives free of diseases that disable and kill.
texts.cdb2761d9ddf: The data supplied by the NHS IC to University of Oxford will be used only for the approved Medical Research Project identified above. UK BioBank aims to study how the health of 500,000 people, currently aged 40-69, from all around the UL is affected by their lifestyle, environment and genes. The purpose of this major project is to improve the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of a wide range of illnesses (such as cancer, heart disease, diabetes, dementia, and joint problems) and to promote health throughout society. By analysing answer, measurements and samples collected from participants, researchers may be able to work out why some people develop particular diseases while others do not. This should help us to find new ways to prevent early death and disability from many different diseases. Like giving blood, UK Biobank is not intended to help directly those who take part – but it should give future generations a much better chance of living free of diseases that disable and kill. The overall purpose of the research is to create a prospective epidemiological resource of 5000,000 people aged 40 -69 from around the UK. The methods to be used for the identification, invitation and assessment of participants have been developed following extensive consultation with leading research groups in the UK and internationally, and with research participants and representatives of the general population. In order to determine the feasibility of the planned approach, two phases of piloting were conducted in 2005 and 2006 (full details are provided in section 1.6.4 of the protocol and in the enclosed integrated pilot report). It is anticipated that as many as 4 million people may need to be approached in order to recruit 500,000 participants in to UK Biobank. Based on previous experience, a centrally coordinated invitation system is considered to be the only viable method to recruit this very large number of participants efficiently within the available budget. UK Biobank’s coordinating centre will obtain contact details for people aged 40 – 69 from NHS data sources in England, Scotland and Wales. The CTSU will process data in confidence on behalf of the NHS, in accordance with the 1998 Data Protection Act, and particular individuals will be provisionally selected for invitation. Immediately prior to invitation mailing, the name, address, gender, date of birth and NHS number (and CHI number in Scotland) of proposed invitees would be sent to ONS for screening against recent death registration to remove the records of people who have recently died in order to help avoid causing upset for relatives who receive an invitation for a recently deceased family member). Subsequently, for the 500,000 consenting participants, follow-up of death, cancer and other health outcomes would be sought from ONS and other health-record systems.

The data supplied by the NHS IC to University of Oxford will be used only for the approved Medical Research Project identified above.  

UK BioBank aims to study how the health of 500,000 people, currently aged 40-69, from all around the UL is affected by their lifestyle, environment and genes. The purpose of this major project is to improve the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of a wide range of illnesses (such as cancer, heart disease, diabetes, dementia, and joint problems) and to promote health throughout society. By analysing answer, measurements and samples collected from participants, researchers may be able to work out why some people develop particular diseases while others do not. This should help us to find new ways to prevent early death and disability from many different diseases. Like giving blood, UK Biobank is not intended to help directly those who take part – but it should give future generations a much better chance of living free of diseases that disable and kill.

The overall purpose of the research is to create a prospective epidemiological resource of 5000,000 people aged 40 -69 from around the UK. The methods to be used for the identification, invitation and assessment of participants have been developed following extensive consultation with leading research groups in the UK and internationally, and with research participants and representatives of the general population. In order to determine the feasibility of the planned approach, two phases of piloting were conducted in 2005 and 2006 (full details are provided in section 1.6.4 of the protocol and in the enclosed integrated pilot report).

It is anticipated that as many as 4 million people may need to be approached in order to recruit 500,000 participants in to UK Biobank. Based on previous experience, a centrally coordinated invitation system is considered to be the only viable method to recruit this very large number of participants efficiently within the available budget. UK Biobank’s coordinating centre will obtain contact details for people aged 40 – 69 from NHS data sources in England, Scotland and Wales.

The CTSU will process data in confidence on behalf of the NHS, in accordance with the 1998 Data Protection Act, and particular individuals will be provisionally selected for invitation. Immediately prior to invitation mailing, the name, address, gender, date of birth and NHS number (and CHI number in Scotland) of proposed invitees would be sent to ONS for screening against recent death registration to remove the records of people who have recently died in order to help avoid causing upset for relatives who receive an invitation for a recently deceased family member).

Subsequently, for the 500,000 consenting participants, follow-up of death, cancer and other health outcomes would be sought from ONS and other health-record systems.
